articles.title: Margaret Hamilton obituary: computer scientist who pioneered software engineering and helped us get to the Moon
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 15 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03233-6Programmer whose forward-thinking and reliable code helped to save the Apollo 11 mission.
articles.content:
Credit: NASA/ZUMA Press/Alamy

Margaret Hamilton — a titan of computer science — has died aged 90. She is best known for her work in developing the software for NASA’s Apollo project, which landed the first humans on the Moon.

Hamilton’s influence on the field of computing was vast. A specialist in systems engineering and human–computer interaction, she helped to develop pioneering techniques for reliable computer programming and is often credited with coining the term ‘software engineering’. Her work on logical procedures and systems that worked even in the presence of errors helped to give software development comparable stature to the development of computer hardware.

The Moon belongs to all of us — not just countries that can afford to reach it

In addition to her work on Apollo at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) in Cambridge, Hamilton ventured out on her own as a software entrepreneur, founding companies that specialized in programming languages and systems used in numerous fields, from space and defence to energy, communications and more.

Hamilton was born Margaret Heafield in Paoli, Indiana, in 1936. Her parents later moved the family to Michigan and encouraged her to explore her considerable talents in both technical and humanities subjects. She began undergraduate studies at the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor before transferring to Earlham College in Richmond, Indiana, where she completed a bachelor of arts in mathematics with a minor in philosophy in 1958.

The next year, Hamilton moved with her first husband, James Cox Hamilton, to Boston, Massachusetts. The two had met at Earlham — he a chemist and the student-body president; she a maths whiz and the homecoming queen, according to their daughter, Lauren. Forgoing her original plan to attend graduate school, Margaret began working with Edward Lorenz, the founder of modern chaos theory — in which tiny variations in large systems can cause major unpredictable changes — in the MIT meteorology department, while James attended law school. With no previous programming experience, Hamilton helped to develop weather-prediction software using the LGP-30, a 31-bit computer with a 4,096-word memory.

In 1961, by then a working mother, Hamilton moved to a new project at the MIT Lincoln Laboratory: coding for the Semi-Automatic Ground Environment (SAGE), a defence system being developed to ward off air attacks by the Soviet Union. Her stellar work on SAGE paid off. When she heard a few years later that a lab on MIT’s main campus was recruiting programmers to send men to the Moon, her application was swiftly advanced. She became the first programmer hired for the Apollo project at MIT, at a time when women made up just a tiny fraction of the workforce in US science and engineering. Although the vast majority of NASA’s Apollo project team was male, Hamilton was joined by a number of women who made key contributions in maths, coding, engineering and more.

First photos from Artemis II: see stunning ‘Earthset’ and more

Hamilton was tapped to head the team tasked with writing and testing software for the Apollo Guidance Computer. The space race was in full swing, and engineers and programmers at the MIT Instrumentation Lab were under high pressure to achieve what had only ever been dreamt of before, both quickly and safely. Hamilton stated in subsequent years that “there was no choice but to be pioneers”.

articles.personality_title: Margaret Hamilton: The computer scientist who helped land humans on the Moon
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Margaret Hamilton was a computer scientist who played a key role in NASA’s Apollo program, which successfully sent astronauts to the Moon in 1969. At a time when few women worked in science and technology, she led the development of software that made the mission possible.

**What happened** – Hamilton passed away at age 90. During the 1960s, she was the first programmer hired for the Apollo project at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT). She led the team that created the software for the Apollo Guidance Computer, which helped guide the spacecraft to the Moon. Her careful work ensured the software could handle unexpected problems during the mission, including a famous moment when the computer alerted astronauts to an overload but still allowed the landing to continue safely.

**Impact** – Hamilton’s work was groundbreaking because she introduced new ideas about writing reliable software, a field that was just beginning. She helped make software engineering a recognized discipline, showing that software could be as carefully designed and tested as hardware. Her ideas are still used today in many areas like space, defense, energy, and communications.

**What's next step** – Hamilton’s legacy continues to inspire new generations of programmers and engineers, especially women in technology. The methods she developed remain important in making software safe and dependable. Her story encourages ongoing efforts to improve how software is created for complex and critical systems.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Margaret Hamilton’s pioneering software work was vital to landing humans on the Moon and shaped the future of reliable computer programming.

articles.title: Why a high school in Virginia is getting a quantum computer
articles.summary: Starting in January, students attending Skyview High School in Virginia will learn about the building blocks and principles underlying quantum computers by working with one directly
articles.content:
A demonstration of the XQ1 at the Quantum World Congress 2026 in Maryland XeedQ

In January, Skyview High School in Virginia will become the first high school in the US to have a quantum computer on its premises. Made by the quantum computing and sensing firm XeedQ, it will be a teaching device aimed at inspiring the next generation of quantum innovators.

The quantum computing industry is in a period of expansion and both governments and private investors are increasing their focus on the field. Yet, many of the industry’s leaders agree that, in addition to investing in quantum technology, there ought to be a concerted effort to grow the quantum workforce as well. Fairfax County Public Schools (FCPS) in Virginia aims to meet this challenge by providing its high school students with hands-on access to a working quantum computer. FCPS Superintendent Michelle Reid says that this is a bet on a career pathway that is “globally exploding” and could set students up for pursuing one of the 800,000 quantum-related jobs projected to be created within the next decade.

The quantum computer, called XQ1, will contain four qubits, or basic building blocks of quantum computation, each of which will be based on a diamond imprinted with specifically designed defects. These types of qubits can operate at room temperature. Gopalakrishnan Balasubramanian at XeedQ says the firm designed XQ1 – which is about the size of a small refrigerator – to be robust enough to withstand the conditions of a classroom and run continuously for several years. He says that XQ1 will cost about $900,000. Reid says that this will still work out cheaper for FCPS than, for instance, a new programme to teach students welding skills.

Advertisement

The computational power of a quantum computer is related to its number of qubits, so XQ1 won’t enable students to run sophisticated programs. Instead, it will allow them to develop intuition for, for example, the probabilistic nature of qubits. Students will be able to test how repeatedly preparing a qubit in one quantum state, equivalent to giving the quantum computer the same inputs over and over, doesn’t necessarily always lead to the same result, or the same output, when the qubit is read out later, says Balasubramanian.

In this way, some of the most fundamental ways in which quantum computers behave differently from conventional computers will become intuitive to students way before they enroll in college and undergo a rigorous formal education in quantum physics, he says. Additionally, students will be able to change electromagnetic pulses that control qubits as well as study the impacts of environmental noise on their functioning. They will work in teams of two or three and learn the coding language Python in the process.

“We anticipate students will work directly with the system and observe the physics in action,” says Reid. She says that XQ1 will initially be part of mathematics and physics classes for students in their last or second to last year of high school, but that the curriculum might expand in future years. Students from other schools in Fairfax county will also have a chance to interact with the machine through weekend programmes, she says. “Our young people are so excited about it,” says Reid.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant educational advancement by placing a quantum computer in a public high school, providing hands-on learning that prepares students for a rapidly growing quantum technology workforce. This has broad societal impact by fostering STEM education and future career pathways in an emerging, high-impact technology sector, with detailed context on the device and educational plans.

articles.title: Google showcases way to fix quantum computer errors more efficiently
articles.summary: Error-proofing the most important operations performed on a quantum computer has so far required lots of resources, but a new experiment shows a more efficient way to make the devices reliable
articles.content:
Error-proofing the most important operations performed on a quantum computer has so far required lots of resources, but a new experiment shows a more efficient way to make the devices reliable

The Willow quantum computer Google Quantum AI

Making quantum computers error-proof is one of the biggest challenges currently facing the technology. Researchers at Google Quantum AI have now demonstrated one way to do so more efficiently. Their work suggests the smaller quantum computers that will be available in the next few years could be more impactful than expected.

Quantum computers can run mathematical operations, analogous to addition or multiplication, that conventional computers cannot. This makes them suitable for solving some problems that had previously been considered unsolvable, such as those that underpin cryptography.

Most important among the quantum operations the computers run are “non-Clifford gates”, which are the key ingredients for algorithms that transcend conventional computation.

Advertisement

But there is a problem. Quantum computers are very error-prone, and their building blocks, called qubits, must be encoded into special groups, or “logical qubits”, before they can execute operations reliably. Executing non-Clifford gates in an error-corrected way requires large numbers of qubits, which means having to build very large quantum computers – a formidable engineering challenge.

Now, Emma Rosenfeld at Google Quantum AI and her colleagues have used the firm’s Willow quantum computer to show that the error-correction process can be made more efficient. Their new technique ultimately reduced Willow’s errors 40 times.

At the centre of their advance is the idea of a “magic state”, which is a special quantum state that qubits must assume before the quantum computer can run error-corrected non-Clifford operations. Creating these states had, so far, been a real bottleneck for quantum computing, says Rosenfeld. “It eats up a lot of qubits and a lot of time,” she says.

Free newsletter Sign up to Professor Hannah Fry’s column Sign up to newsletter

In 2024, her colleagues at Google Quantum AI proposed a more efficient method for creating magic states called “magic state cultivation”. Here, instead of many imperfect qubits being repeatedly combined and manipulated into a magic state that is then put towards running an error-corrected operation, the magic state is “grown” within a smaller patch of qubits.

The Google researchers showed that magic state cultivation could, in theory, enable quantum computers to run consequential programs with just one-tenth the number of qubits we had expected they would need. The new experiment by Rosenfeld and her colleagues proves that magic state cultivation works in practice.

This is not the first time that new methods for making magic states have lowered a quantum computer’s error rates. Advances in creating magic states and error-correcting non-Clifford gates have also been achieved in experiments with quantum computers that have qubits based on ions. Willow’s qubits, which are based on tiny superconducting circuits, achieved error rates similar to those past experiments, but Rosenfeld says that they work more quickly, potentially reducing the quantum computer’s overall runtime.

“This is an impressive demonstration of a promising recent idea pioneered by Google,” says Isaac Kim at the University of California, Davis. “It’s an approach that can make fault-tolerant quantum computing substantially cheaper.” The new work demonstrates one of the building blocks necessary for universal quantum computing and could be a “gamechanger” in terms of building intermediately sized quantum computers with hundreds of logical qubits, says Dominik Hangleiter at ETH Zurich in Switzerland.

Zhenyu Cai at Imperial College London says that while this experiment is a significant step forward, Willow’s errors will need to be reduced further before it can tackle truly useful problems. Additionally, Kim says that in the experiment, Willow generated good magic states only for a fraction of its computational runs: only 8 per cent of Willow’s computations produced high-quality magic states that could then be put into further use.

Rosenfeld says that this percentage ought to increase as she and her colleagues refine the technique and improve Willow’s hardware. It is, in this case, also affected by a very careful benchmarking technique that the team used, which may not be used in future applications, she says. “This is the first demonstration that the concepts work. We’re not done.”
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant technological breakthrough in quantum computing error correction, demonstrating a more efficient method that could make quantum computers more practical and impactful in the near future. This advancement has broad implications for computing power and problem-solving capabilities beyond current limits, with detailed context and expert commentary supporting its significance.

articles.title: World’s timekeepers upend how they adjust time to avoid catastrophic ‘negative second’
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 15 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03329-zGovernments have voted to abolish the leap second immediately and replace it with a leap hour.
articles.content:
Metrologists retire the leap second immediately, instead of by 2035. Credit: Alejandro Martinez Velez/Europa Press via Getty

Time discrepancies that used to be adjusted by a jump of a second around once every 1.5 years will now wait until an hour needs correcting instead.

Leap seconds serve to align time given by the sun’s position in the sky, which is based on Earth’s unsteady natural rotation, with the more stable ticking of atomic clocks, known as Universal Coordinated Time (UTC). But the rogue seconds have been a thorn in timekeepers' sides, disrupting computing systems and causing misalignment between clocks on the day they are implemented.

Their replacement — a shift of an hour once Earth time and atomic time drift apart by 3,600 seconds — likely won’t be needed for thousands of years, effectively pushing the issue onto future generations.

The leap second is dead. Long live the leap hour?

Member states of the General Conference on Weights and Measures (CGPM) voted to pass the resolution at their 28th meeting, outside Paris, on 15 October.

“This decision will ensure the continuity and relevance of UTC for centuries to come,” says Georgette Macdonald, director general of the National Research Council of Canada’s Metrology Research Centre in Halifax, Canada. Canada backed the resolution, which was not supported unanimously but only needed a majority to pass, she says.

“This is a historical moment, a decisive step for UTC”, says Noël Dimarcq, a metrologist at the Côte d'Azur Observatory in Nice, France, who formally introduced the resolution. "We now have an international reference time scale [that is] continuous for the next millennia", he adds.

articles.personality_title: International decision ends leap seconds, introduces leap hour for timekeeping
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – For decades, leap seconds have been added occasionally to clocks to keep time aligned with Earth's rotation. This is because atomic clocks run very steadily, but Earth’s spin is uneven. Leap seconds helped match these two, but they caused problems for computers and other systems.

**What happened** – On October 15, 2026, the General Conference on Weights and Measures (CGPM), a group of countries that set global time standards, voted to stop using leap seconds immediately. Instead, they will add a leap hour when needed, which will happen far less often—likely thousands of years from now.

**Impact** – This change means fewer disruptions to technology and more stable timekeeping. Computers and networks will no longer face sudden one-second jumps that can cause errors. It also sets a continuous time system that will work smoothly for centuries, helping scientists and industries that depend on precise timing.

**What's next step** – The new system will be put into practice right away. Countries and organizations will update their clocks and technology to follow this rule. In the very long term, when Earth’s rotation slows enough to require it, a leap hour will be added instead of a leap second.

**One-sentence takeaway** – The world has stopped using leap seconds and will add a leap hour only after thousands of years, making timekeeping simpler and more reliable for the future.

articles.personality_title_es: Los relojes mundiales eliminan el segundo bisiesto y adoptan una hora bisiesta
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Durante décadas, se han añadido segundos bisiestos para mantener el tiempo alineado con la rotación irregular de la Tierra. Los relojes atómicos son muy precisos, pero la Tierra gira de forma desigual. Estos segundos causaban problemas a computadoras y otros sistemas.

**Qué pasó** – El 15 de octubre de 2026, la Conferencia General de Pesas y Medidas (CGPM), un grupo de países que establece normas globales de tiempo, votó para eliminar inmediatamente el uso de segundos bisiestos. En su lugar, se añadirá una hora bisiesta cuando sea necesario, lo que ocurrirá mucho menos seguido, probablemente en miles de años.

**Impacto** – Este cambio reduce interrupciones tecnológicas y asegura un tiempo más estable. Las computadoras ya no sufrirán saltos de un segundo que causaban errores. Esto crea un sistema de tiempo continuo que funcionará sin problemas durante siglos, ayudando a científicos e industrias que dependen de un tiempo exacto.

**Próximo paso** – El nuevo sistema se implementará de inmediato. Los países y organizaciones actualizarán sus relojes y tecnología para seguir esta regla. A muy largo plazo, cuando la rotación de la Tierra se desacelere lo suficiente, se añadirá una hora bisiesta en lugar de un segundo.

**Resumen en una frase** – El mundo deja de usar segundos bisiestos y añadirá una hora bisiesta solo dentro de miles de años, haciendo la medición del tiempo más simple y confiable para el futuro.
